column5: lost travelers, straight route, inhabited city
column6: The commentary asks God to guide a traveler along a road that reaches an accepting home; the psalm says God led desert wanderers by a straight way to a city in which to dwell.

column5: guided return beside waters, level nonstumbling path
column6: Against the commentary's guide, water, and steady upright walking, God leads returning Israel beside streams on a level path where they will not stumble.

column5: prayer for light and truth to lead to God's dwelling
column6: Like ihdinā as a direct plea for a road ending with God, the psalmist asks that God's light and truth lead him to the holy hill and dwelling.

column5: lead me, make the way straight, hostile watchers
column6: The commentary joins a supplication for the straight path to an ambush on it; this prayer asks God to lead the speaker in righteousness and make the way straight because of enemies watching him.

column5: teach your way, level path, enemies
column6: The commentary's guided walker needs an unbending road under threat; the psalm petitions God to teach his way and lead on a level path because of adversaries.

column5: God makes a person's paths straight
column6: The commentary treats guidance as more than receiving a map; Proverbs makes acknowledging God in all one's ways the setting in which he straightens the person's paths.

column5: teacher leads pupil in upright paths
column6: The commentary's guide both introduces the road and walks it with the traveler; Wisdom says it has taught the way of wisdom and led its pupil in paths of uprightness.

column5: blind travelers, unknown paths, darkness made light
column6: The commentary includes lost travelers, signs, and a guide who knows the road; God leads blind people on unknown ways, makes darkness light, and levels rough ground.

column5: continual guidance, water, bodily strength
column6: The commentary says guidance must be requested again at every step and pairs uprightness with water and support; this promise says the Lord will guide continually, satisfy drought, and strengthen the body like a watered garden.

column5: God goes before Israel, cloud and fire guide the way
column6: The commentary's hâdî is an antecedent rather than a detached map; in the wilderness the Lord goes before Israel visibly to lead them by day and night.

column5: shepherd leading to waters of rest
column6: The commentary draws together flock, guide, water, and rest from swaying travel; the shepherd leads the sheep to waters of rest.

column5: shepherd guides in paths of righteousness
column6: The commentary's requested straight road is lived under a leading guide; the shepherd restores and guides the sheep in righteous paths for his name.

column5: God the shepherd gathers and brings the flock to pasture
column6: The commentary's front-going guide and flock move toward a place of provision; God as shepherd brings scattered Israel from the nations into its land and pasture.

column5: voice says this is the way, walk in it
column6: The commentary develops direction as an orientation that must be renewed while walking; Isaiah gives the traveler a divine voice from behind that identifies the way at each turn.

column5: highway of holiness where travelers do not go astray
column6: The commentary contrasts the road that carries a traveler with the loss named in 1:7; Isaiah's holy highway is specifically a way on which even travelers do not wander.

column5: level track for the feet, secure ways
column6: The commentary's upright path is a continuing bodily gait rather than immobility; Proverbs tells the hearer to level the track for the feet so that all ways are secure.

column5: God led a servant by the right way to a bride
column6: The commentary's h-d-y image includes leading a bride to her husband's house; Abraham's servant blesses God for leading him by the right way to obtain Rebekah for Isaac.

column5: Arabic q-w-m and Hebrew qwm, made to walk upright
column6: The commentary explicitly develops ق و م as upright walking; the cognate Hebrew qwm appears in God's making liberated Israel walk upright, supplying a concrete bodily use rather than a dictionary comparison.

column5: communal ascent, God teaches ways, people walk paths
column6: The praying plural of the commentary seeks a road inseparable from worship; the nations say together that they will go to God's house so that he may teach his ways and they may walk his paths.

column5: just scales and weights
column6: The commentary makes mustaqīm audible as a scale that leans to neither side; Leviticus makes honest balances and weights a commanded form of covenantal uprightness.

column5: level path of the righteous made level by the Just One
column6: The commentary's straightness combines moral rightness with a physically level road; Isaiah calls the righteous person's path level and attributes its leveling to God.

column5: lamp for feet and light for a path
column6: The commentary's traveler finds a road by signs rather than walking blindly; the psalm makes God's word a lamp for the feet and light for the path.

column5: a walker's steps are not self-directed
column6: The commentary insists that the needy traveler asks the one who can truly guide; Jeremiah says a person's way is not in himself and that a walker cannot direct his own steps.

column5: God instructs, teaches, and counsels the way
column6: The commentary distinguishes being shown the road from being led upon it; the psalm's divine speaker promises instruction, teaching in the way to go, and watchful counsel.

column5: good spirit leads onto level ground
column6: The commentary connects ongoing prayer, support, and an unbending route; the psalm asks God's good spirit to lead the petitioner into level land.

column5: guidance by counsel followed by reception
column6: The commentary hears the road as ending where the traveler is received by God; the psalm explicitly joins God's present counsel-guidance to being received afterward in glory.

column5: strength in God and pilgrimage roads in the heart
column6: The commentary's traveler needs divine support while moving toward the house; this pilgrimage blessing locates strength in God and the highways to Zion in the worshiper's heart.

column5: God teaches and leads in the way one should go
column6: The commentary says guidance belongs to God and is both instruction and movement; Isaiah names God as the teacher for benefit and the one who leads on the proper way.

column5: guarding a traveler in all their ways
column6: The commentary's straight road remains a place of ambush and need for help; the psalm depicts God's angels guarding the faithful person in all his ways.

column5: walk the whole commanded way for life
column6: The commentary says worship of God is itself the straight road and is sustained rather than attained once; Deuteronomy commands Israel to walk the whole divine way so that it may live and flourish.

column5: Traveler's Prayer: lead us, direct our steps, bring us to destination
column6: The commentary's plural direct request for guidance and arrival has a close Jewish liturgical counterpart in the Traveler's Prayer, which asks God to lead us in peace, direct our steps, and bring us to the desired destination.

column5: ask God that ways be made straight
column6: The commentary makes guidance a repeated prayer rather than a past conversion; Tobit's father tells his son to bless God continually and ask that his ways be made straight.

column5: wisdom straightens earthly paths and teaches God's pleasure
column6: The commentary treats hidayet as divine gift and instruction in a road; Wisdom says that human paths were made straight and people learned what pleases God through wisdom.

column5: Isaiah's desert road interpreted as Torah discipline
column6: The commentary identifies worship and continuing conduct with the straight road; the Community Rule rereads Isaiah's prepared wilderness way as a separated community's study and practice of Torah.

column5: guide our feet into the way of peace
column6: The commentary's guide brings walkers toward the abode of peace; Zechariah's song asks the dawning light to guide feet into the way of peace.

column5: plural prayer against testing and the Evil One
column6: Like ihdinā after a communal address to God, the Lord's Prayer uses the plural to ask that God not lead the petitioners into testing and rescue them from the Evil One.

column5: restricted road leading to life
column6: The commentary treats the road as a lived route whose end matters; Jesus contrasts the constricted road that leads to life with the broad road ending in destruction.

column5: shepherd goes ahead and sheep follow his voice
column6: The commentary's hâdî walks in front of a flock rather than merely pointing; Jesus' shepherd goes ahead of his own sheep, who follow because they know his voice.

column5: way to the Father
column6: The commentary says the straight road leads to God and an abiding home; Jesus identifies himself as the way by which one comes to the Father.

column5: Spirit of truth will guide into all truth
column6: The commentary rejects a one-time model of guidance; Jesus promises future, continuing guidance by the Spirit of truth into the whole truth.

column5: straight paths for feet so the lame may be healed
column6: The commentary pictures a weak, swaying walker needing help before a calm upright gait; Hebrews calls for straight tracks for the feet so that the lame are healed rather than turned aside.

column5: straying sheep return to Shepherd and Overseer
column6: The commentary sets the guided flock against those who lose the road; Peter describes people who had wandered like sheep and now return to their Shepherd and Guardian.

column5: leaving the straight way and wandering after Balaam
column6: The commentary stresses that guidance can be lost after it is received; Peter describes false teachers who abandoned the straight way and wandered after Balaam.

column5: Lamb shepherds and guides to springs of living water
column6: The commentary brings together guide, flock, water, and the road's final welcome; Revelation has the Lamb shepherd the faithful and guide them to springs of living water.

column5: Lord strengthens and guards from the Evil One
column6: The commentary pairs the request for help with the road where the adversary lies in wait; Paul names the faithful Lord as the one who strengthens and guards believers from the Evil One.

column5: Isaiah's straight road applied to John preparing the Lord
column6: The commentary treats a road as preparation for divine encounter; Mark reuses Isaiah's road-making oracle to interpret John's wilderness ministry as preparing the Lord's way.

column5: two ways: life and death
column6: The commentary contrasts the one straight road with paths that lose their travelers; the Didache opens its moral instruction with two distinct ways, one of life and one of death.

column5: new and living way through sacrificial access
column6: The commentary's road ends at a holy accepting place and includes an offering brought to its destination; Hebrews calls Christ's sacrificial access to God's presence a new and living way.

column5: offering brought to sanctuary for acceptance
column6: The commentary's h-d-y images include a sacrificial animal reaching its assigned sacred place; Leviticus requires the herd offering at the tent entrance so that it is accepted before God.

column5: weighed in a just balance so integrity is known
column6: The commentary uses an unequally leaning scale to make moral straightness audible; Job asks to be weighed on just scales so that God may know his integrity.

column5: crossroads, ancient paths, the good way
column6: The commentary sets one straight road against dispersing paths; Jeremiah tells the people at the crossroads to ask for the ancient paths, find the good way, and walk in it.

column5: God knows the righteous way; the wicked way perishes
column6: The commentary's next verse distinguishes the given road from those who are lost; Psalm 1 frames the moral contrast as the way God knows and the way that comes to ruin.

column5: God led the whole wilderness journey to test and teach
column6: The commentary says the already guided still ask for guidance at every stage; Moses tells Israel to remember the whole wilderness route by which God led it over many years.

column5: walking humbly with God
column6: The commentary says direct worship becomes a way of upright life; Micah condenses the required response to justice, faithful love, and a humble walk with God.

column5: a person is led in the way he wishes to go
column6: The commentary holds together God's guidance and the possibility of choosing blindness or losing the way; the Talmud formulates that people are led along the path they choose.

column5: walking after God interpreted as imitating merciful acts
column6: The commentary makes the road an embodied form of worship, not only a direction; Sotah reads walking after God as concrete imitation of God's merciful deeds.

column5: Prince of Lights and paths of light versus darkness
column6: The commentary's single guide and divergent paths acquire a Second Temple moral cosmology here: the righteous walk paths of light under the Prince of Lights, in contrast to darkness.

column5: narrow perilous path between fire and water
column6: The commentary explicitly resists reducing sirat to a postmortem bridge; 4 Ezra instead imagines access to the good city through a single perilous, narrow path between fire and water.

column5: the straight path a person should choose
column6: The commentary expands straightness into balanced moral conduct; Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi asks which straight path one should choose and answers with a course that brings honor before God and people.

column5: Lord direct hearts into love and steadfastness
column6: The commentary's istiqāmah is sustained standing after a confession; Paul asks the Lord to direct believers' hearts into God's love and Christ's steadfastness.

column5: God and Jesus direct our way
column6: The commentary includes a literal traveler asking for a route as well as moral guidance; Paul prays that God and the Lord Jesus themselves direct the apostles' way to the Thessalonians.

column5: how can I understand unless someone guides me?
column6: The commentary contrasts a guide who knows the way with a person unable to find it alone; the Ethiopian applies that need to reading Isaiah, asking how he can understand without a guide.

column5: Lord's Prayer prescribed three times daily
column6: The commentary treats the plural plea for guidance as renewed daily rather than once for all; the Didache orders the community to pray the Lord's Prayer, with its request for deliverance, three times a day.

column5: the Father draws the one who comes to Jesus
column6: The commentary says that ultimate guidance belongs to God rather than even to a beloved human guide; John makes coming to Jesus dependent on the Father's drawing action.

column5: angel sent ahead to guard the way and bring Israel to a prepared place
column6: The commentary's guide goes before the weak traveler and brings the road to its appointed home; God sends an angel before Israel to guard it on the way and bring it to the place prepared.

column5: communal fast to seek from God a straight way
column6: The commentary's plural petition asks God directly for the straight path; Ezra proclaims a communal fast to seek from God a straight way for us, the children, and the journey's goods.

column5: ark goes ahead so Israel knows an untraveled way
column6: The commentary says guidance is following a precursor rather than holding a map; Israel lets the ark go before it so that it may know a route it has never traveled.

column5: compassionate guide leads to springs of water
column6: The commentary connects guidance, water, and protection on the journey; Isaiah's compassionate God leads and guides the people by springs so that hunger, thirst, and scorching sun do not overwhelm them.

column5: lost sheep made to wander by their shepherds
column6: The commentary contrasts the guide who knows the path with one who cannot lead and the flock that becomes lost; Jeremiah calls the people lost sheep whose shepherds caused them to wander and forget their resting place.

column5: way in wilderness and rivers in desert
column6: The commentary's straight road is both a route for a traveler and a life-giving course with water; God promises a new way in wilderness and rivers in the desert.

column5: valleys raised, rough ground leveled, crooked made straight
column6: The commentary expands mustaqīm through uprightness, leveling, and an unequally leaning scale; Isaiah's prepared divine road is made by raising, lowering, straightening, and smoothing its terrain.

column5: crooked paths, no justice, no way of peace
column6: The commentary joins straightness, just balance, and the abode of peace; Isaiah describes the inverse, where those without justice make crooked paths and do not know the way of peace.

column5: righteous walk the Lord's right ways; transgressors stumble
column6: The commentary's path is right not merely by name but because it carries its walkers upright while the lost fall away; Hosea says the Lord's ways are right, the righteous walk in them, and transgressors stumble.

column5: lost sheep asks God to seek the servant
column6: The commentary's flock has a guide while 1:7 names those who lose the road; the psalm ends by admitting, like a lost sheep, the need for God to seek the servant.

column5: examination followed by a plea to lead in the everlasting way
column6: The commentary treats guidance as a prayer renewed even by people already addressing God; this psalm asks God to expose a harmful way in the speaker and then lead him in the enduring way.

column5: a way that seems right but ends in death
column6: The commentary insists that a road's destination distinguishes it from a mere direction; Proverbs warns that a path appearing right to a person can nevertheless end in death.

column5: trust, divine help, and making ways straight
column6: The commentary pairs the request for help with the request for the straight road; Sirach tells the hearer to trust God for help and to make the ways straight in hope.

column5: Wisdom guides a fleeing righteous person on straight paths
column6: The commentary develops guidance as accompanying a literal traveler and bringing one toward God's realm; personified Wisdom guides a righteous fugitive on straight paths and shows him God's kingdom.

column5: a good angel accompanies the journey and returns the traveler safely
column6: The commentary's guide goes with a traveler toward a homeward destination; Tobit's reassurance is that a good angel will accompany Tobiah, make the journey succeed, and bring him back safely.

column5: traveler turns body or heart toward the Holy of Holies
column6: The commentary treats direction and direct prayer as inseparable even for a moving traveler; the Mishnah directs a rider who cannot face the sanctuary bodily to direct the heart toward it.

column5: following the light avoids darkness and gains life's light
column6: The commentary's guide leads a traveler who might otherwise be lost in darkness; Jesus says that whoever follows him will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life.

column5: walking in light before darkness overtakes and obscures the destination
column6: The commentary's road has markers and can be lost; Jesus warns listeners to walk while they have the light, because the one walking in darkness does not know where he is going.

column5: worshiping God according to the Way
column6: The commentary says worship of God is itself the straight road; Paul describes his worship of Israel's God as taking place according to the Way that opponents call a sect.

column5: God keeps the traveler wherever he goes and brings him home
column6: The commentary's road ends in a place of acceptance and needs help along the way; God promises Jacob presence and protection wherever he goes, followed by return to the promised land.

column5: God provides a way out of testing that can be endured
column6: The commentary puts divine help beside a path where the adversary waits; Paul describes God as making a way out within testing so that believers can endure it.

column5: Abraham obeys a call to go without knowing the destination
column6: The commentary rejects a merely detached map in favor of being led along a road; Abraham goes in obedience to God's call even though he does not know where he is going.

column5: Christ leaves an example so believers follow his steps
column6: The commentary's guide advances before those who follow; Peter makes Christ's suffering an exemplar whose steps believers are called to follow.
